Here's something that surprises most people: an LLM never actually sees your words. It sees numbers.

Before your prompt reaches the model, it gets chopped into pieces called **tokens**, chunks that are often whole words but can also be word fragments or punctuation.

Each token is then swapped for a number from a fixed list. GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens, so "cat" becomes one number, "sat" another.

[EX]Take the sentence "The cat sat on the mat." A tokenizer might split it into pieces like "The", " cat", " sat", " on", " the", " mat", ".", and turn each into an ID such as 464, 3797, 3332... (these numbers are made up for illustration, since every tokenizer uses different ones).[/EX]

[KEY]An LLM works on a sequence of numbers (tokens), not on words or meanings directly.[/KEY]

[Q]
Why does a language model convert your text into tokens and numbers first?
A) Because the model can only do math on numbers, not on raw text
B) Because numbers let it translate your prompt into another language
C) Because it looks each word up in a database of stored answers
ANS: A
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked A) Because the model can only do math on numbers, not on raw text
replies.raw:
Right: everything the model does is arithmetic, so text has to become numbers before anything else can happen.

Now for what the numbers become. Each token ID is turned into a long list of numbers called an **embedding**, and similar meanings end up with similar lists, like neighbors on a giant map.

But a single token's embedding can't settle its meaning on its own. That's the job of **attention**: each token looks back at the words before it and adjusts itself based on what it finds.

[EX]Take the word "bank". In "We walked along the river and sat down on the bank", attention to "river" pulls it toward a riverside meaning. In "I put cash in the bank", attention to "cash" pulls it toward money.[/EX]

[KEY]Attention lets the surrounding words decide what each token means in context.[/KEY]

[Q]
In "I put cash in the bank", what makes the model treat "bank" as a money bank?
A) Attention to the earlier word "cash" shifts its meaning
B) The tokenizer gives it a different ID for the money sense
C) It searches the internet for what "bank" means here
ANS: A
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) The tokenizer gives it a different ID for the money sense
replies.raw:
Not quite, and this is a really common mix-up.

The tokenizer works before any meaning is figured out. It sees the letters "bank" and hands back the same token ID every time, whether you mean money or a river.

So the sorting happens later, inside the model. Attention looks at "cash" or "river" earlier in the sentence and shifts that one shared token toward the right meaning.

Here's a different case. The word "bat" gets one token, whether it's a baseball bat or the flying animal. In "The bat flew out of the cave at dusk", the model works out which one you mean from the words around it.

[KEY]Same word, same token ID; the context words decide the meaning through attention.[/KEY]

[Q]
In "The bat flew out of the cave at dusk", how does the model tell which kind of "bat" this is?
A) The tokenizer assigns a different ID to the animal sense
B) Attention to nearby words like "flew" and "cave" shifts its meaning
C) The model looks up "bat" in a table of definitions
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) Attention to nearby words like "flew" and "cave" shifts its meaning
replies.raw:
Yes, that's it. Same token ID for "bat", and the surrounding words do the sorting.

Now the last piece, and it's the step that produces the words you see. After attention has shaped the meaning of everything in your prompt, the model does one job: it scores every token in its vocabulary by how likely it is to come next. This is **next-token prediction**.

The result is a probability for each candidate. The model picks one (usually a likely one), adds it to the text, and then repeats the whole process to get the following token. A full reply is built one token at a time.

[EX]Take "The cat sat on the ___". The model might give "mat" a high probability, "floor" and "sofa" smaller ones, and "democracy" almost none. When one continuation dominates, the model is confident. When many fit, the probability is spread out.[/EX]

[KEY]An LLM writes by repeatedly predicting a probability for each possible next token, then picking one.[/KEY]

[Q]
For "The capital of France is ___", what would the model's next-token probabilities most likely look like?
A) Probability is spread evenly across thousands of tokens
B) The model has no preference until it searches for the answer
C) One token ("Paris") gets nearly all the probability
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) One token ("Paris") gets nearly all the probability
replies.raw:
Yes. When the pattern is that strong, one token takes almost all the probability, and the model is highly confident. Notice it wasn't looking anything up.

"Paris" simply dominates what usually follows that phrase.

That covers the whole path: your text becomes tokens, tokens become embeddings, attention adjusts each one using the words before it, and the model predicts the next token, over and over.

Now let's put this to work. Here are three sentences, each ending in a blank where the model must predict the next word:

1. "Water freezes at zero degrees ___"
2. "My favorite thing to do on a weekend is ___"
3. "The cat sat on the ___"

For each one, say whether the model's top prediction would be **high confidence** (one word dominates) or **low confidence** (many words fit). Then explain why, in terms of how the probability would be spread across possible next tokens.

[Q]
